newsitem.title: GERMANY: Analyst comment on Bonn-Buba forex reserves deal.
newsitem.headline: Analyst comment on Bonn-Buba forex reserves deal.

text.p: Following are comments from economists on news that Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer and German Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Thursday reached a pact on revaluing the central bank's currency reserves.
The German central bank will use room provided by the Maastricht Treaty to revalue its foreign exchange reserves nearer to market prices in 1997 using accounting rules in existing law.
The measure is expected to allow for a payout of booked profits to Bonn in the 1998 fiscal year.
THOMAS MAYER, SENIOR ECONOMIST, GOLDMAN SACHS, FRANKFURT:
"Initially it seems to be in line with what we have expected. The speculation has been that it would allow Bonn to transfer up to 13 billion marks in 1998 of forex reserves.

"The speculation on gold reserves has been that it would take place only in 1999 when the European Central Bank would establish the principles of the revaluation. They would then be able to use the proceeds to pay down Germany's debt. That would obviously require a change in Bundesbank law."
GERHARD GREBE, CHIEF ECONOMIST, BANK JULIUS BAER, FRANKFURT:

"This may be significant for Waigel and his budget but it is not really significant for the markets. I think it was clear that there would be an agreement. Both sides had signalled that this would be so.

"This seems to indicate that currency reserves will be revalued to a higher level without compromising the minimum evaluation principle. That might mean that the dollar would be revalued to the lowest level it reached this year, which would still keep it in touch with the market value."
Grebe said, for example, that some seven billion marks could be yielded for the 1998 budget if dollar reserves were to be to be revalued to 1.50 marks.

"Of course this will not be enough to plug the budget gap. But what it does do is ensure a continued high payout to Bonn from the Bundesbank. This year, the transfer was reduced because of low interest rates."
Hermann Remsperger, chief economist, BHF-Bank in Frankfurt:

"I would say the statement was in line with expectations. It has two elements, firstly the revaluation of the dollar reserves and secondly a reorganisation of the Bundesbank's capital structure. It is true that 1997 is the basis for the choice of which nations will enter European monetary union but one should take note that nations' budget plans for 1998 will also be taken into account. The question is whether the increased profit transfer to the government will be relevant to the deficit calculation for Maastricht. It is still unclear on what basis the currency reserves will be valued. It will depend on the assessment of currency market conditions in 1998."
